meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who opens a school door, closes a prison'?
meta.ogDescription: This school-and-prison line isn't in any of Victor Hugo's actual works. Here's who probably said it first.

answer.label: Not Victor Hugo — actually Louis-Charles Jourdan
answer.sourceLine: This school-and-prison aphorism has been pinned on Victor Hugo since the nineteenth century, but Hugo's own research group finds it in none of his writings; the wording traces instead to journalist Louis-Charles Jourdan, recorded in Pierre Larousse’s Grand dictionnaire universel du XIXe siècle.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Ouvrir une école aujourd’hui, c’est fermer une prison dans vingt ans.”
Pierre Larousse, Grand dictionnaire universel du XIXe siècle, vol. VII (1870) & vol. XIII (1875)
“He who opens a school door, closes a prison” (translator and date unrecorded)

source.excerpt: Ouvrir une école aujourd’hui, c’est fermer une prison dans vingt ans.
trail: Long credited to Victor Hugo, but the Hugo research group Groupe Hugo concludes the formula is found nowhere in his work.
The earliest citations instead credit the idea to Victor Duruy, France’s Minister of Public Instruction, in 1865, per Wikiquote’s sourced Misattributed entry.
The specific wording was recorded by Pierre Larousse as belonging to journalist Louis-Charles Jourdan, whose biography confirms the Hugo misattribution.
A history of the Cherche-Midi prison notes the saying was already treated as a well-worn, disputed slogan by 1929, according to a study of French penitentiary history.
source.excerptNote: The original French names a specific time frame — “in twenty years” — that the popular English version drops, along with its reference to a specific act rather than the generic “he who.”

sourceLink.text: Groupe Hugo: the true origin of the school/prison formula

source.rightsNote: The original French line was published in the 1870s and is long out of copyright, but the exact translator and date behind the popular English wording “he who opens a school door, closes a prison” are unrecorded, so this specific rendering’s status can’t be confirmed.

author.name: Louis-Charles Jourdan
author.heading: About Louis-Charles Jourdan
author.bio: Jourdan was a Toulon-born journalist aligned with Saint-Simonian and phalansterian circles who became one of the most-read contributors to the Parisian daily Le Siècle from 1849 onward. He was briefly imprisoned in 1851 for an article criticizing Louis-Napoléon’s government before returning to a long career in the French press.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most persistently misattributed lines in French letters — it has been pinned on at least three different men since the 1860s before researchers traced it to a little-known journalist.

items.why: The earliest documented citations tie the idea to Duruy rather than Hugo: “Déjà M. Duruy avait posé en fait, qu’ouvrir une école, c’est fermer une prison” (1865), per Wikiquote’s sourced record.
French Hugo scholars trace still more attributions to the medievalist-deputy Jubinal and the British historian Macaulay before the trail leads to Jourdan, according to the Groupe Hugo research site.
Quote sites and merchandise still credit Hugo by default, even though no reliable source confirms he is the author.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-documented trail leads to journalist Louis-Charles Jourdan of Le Siècle, whose 1870s wording was recorded by Pierre Larousse — not to Victor Hugo, per Jourdan’s biography.

context.heading: A Republican rallying cry
lead: By the 1860s, the claim that opening schools would empty prisons had become a slogan of France’s Republican education reformers, who argued that free, compulsory schooling was the best defense against poverty-driven crime.

Victor Hugo championed the same connection between education and crime in his own words elsewhere in his career, which is likely why this borrowed slogan stuck to his name long after its actual author, journalist Louis-Charles Jourdan, was forgotten.
